title: HTTP: requests, methods, status codes
story:
Two programs that were never built together need a shared vocabulary for asking and answering. The vocabulary has three parts: a verb saying what kind of action is intended, a number saying what happened, and a header area for everything that does not fit in either.

The current specification of the semantics is RFC 9110, published in June 2022 as Standard 97, and it describes the protocol as a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems, defining the request methods, response status codes and header fields. Note which document that is, because the citation situation here is unusually bad. RFC 9110 obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615 and 7694 along with portions of 7230. The one everybody learned from, RFC 2616 of 1999, was superseded first by a six-document series in 2014 and then reorganised again in 2022. Specifications still pointing at 2616 or 7231 are citing documents that have been obsolete for years, and that includes some very widely used ones.

The reorganisation is the interesting part, and it is a piece of design rather than bookkeeping. The semantics were separated from the wire format deliberately, so that each major protocol version can progress independently while referring to the same core semantics. All three major versions rely on the semantics defined in that one document, and none has obsoleted the others, because each has specific benefits and limitations depending on the context of use.

Read what that implies, because it is the thing most people get wrong about the newer versions. The verbs and the numbers are version-independent. A request to retrieve a resource means exactly the same thing in every version; a status code means exactly the same thing in every version. What the newer versions changed is how the bytes are laid out and how connections are managed — binary framing, multiplexing many exchanges over one connection, compressing the headers, and in the newest case moving to a different transport entirely. The application-visible vocabulary did not change at all.

That separation is why upgrading is usually invisible to application code and yet changes performance characteristics substantially. Your handler still receives the same verb and returns the same number. What changes underneath is how many round trips were needed, whether one slow response blocks others queued behind it, and how much of each request is header repetition. Code that was written against the performance behaviour of an older version — bundling many small resources into one, sharding across hostnames — is optimising against a constraint that may no longer exist.

problem.name: A uniform application protocol
problem.shape: Two independently built programs need a shared way to ask for things and report what happened, general enough that neither knows the other's internals.
tell: a client and server are being designed together and a bespoke protocol is tempting
status codes are being chosen by what looks reasonable
a performance workaround was inherited from an older version
documentation cites a specification number without checking it is current
problem.move: Use the verbs and numbers for what they mean rather than as decoration, since intermediaries act on them. Check which document defines the semantics you are relying on, because several widely cited ones are obsolete. And separate what your code depends on — the semantics — from what the transport does, which changes between versions.
problem.invariant: The semantics are defined once and shared by every version. Methods and status codes mean the same thing regardless of how the bytes are framed on the wire.
problem.breaks: The vocabulary is only as meaningful as the honesty of its use. Nothing enforces that a verb declared safe does not change state, or that a success code accompanies an actual success, and caches and intermediaries act on those declarations — so a dishonest response is not merely unclear, it is acted upon by machinery you do not control.

cost.time: a general vocabulary carries fields most exchanges do not need, which is what header compression in the newer versions exists to claw back
cost.beats: a bespoke protocol, which is smaller and forfeits every intermediary — caches, proxies, gateways and tooling all act on the standard vocabulary and can do nothing with a private one

worked.problem: What actually changed between the major versions of this protocol?
worked.reasoning:
The wire format and the connection handling. Not the semantics — and the separation is deliberate rather than incidental.

The specification was reorganised so that semantics live in one document and the message syntax in others, expressly so that each major protocol version can progress independently while referring to the same core semantics. All three major versions rely on the semantics defined in that one document, and none has obsoleted the others because each has specific benefits and limitations depending on the context of use.

So the things application code touches are unchanged. A method means what it meant. A status code means what it meant. Header fields have the same semantics. If you write a handler, it receives the same vocabulary regardless of which version carried it, which is why an upgrade is usually invisible in application code.

What changed is underneath. The second major version replaced the text framing with a binary one, allowed many exchanges to be multiplexed over a single connection rather than queued, and compressed headers, because a general vocabulary repeated on every request is a real cost. The third moved to a different transport, which removes a layer of ordering that was causing one lost packet to stall exchanges that had nothing to do with it.

The reason this matters practically is not trivia. Performance characteristics changed substantially while the interface did not, and a large amount of received wisdom is optimisation against the older constraints. Bundling many small resources into one file, sharding assets across hostnames, minimising the number of requests — those were responses to a version where connections were scarce and requests queued. Under multiplexing they range from unnecessary to harmful. Code inherits the workaround long after the constraint is gone.

I would also flag the citation problem, because it bites. The document most people learned from is two reorganisations out of date: it was superseded by a six-document series and then those were consolidated again, so specifications and tooling still pointing at the old numbers are citing things obsolete for years. When the precise behaviour of a method or a code matters, it is worth checking which document actually defines it now.

problem.practice: Find a performance practice in your codebase that exists to reduce the number of requests, and work out which protocol version it was written for. Then check which version your clients actually negotiate. Separately, grep your specifications and documentation for the obsolete numbers.

beats.broke: Two programs that were never built together need a shared vocabulary for asking and answering, general enough that neither has to know the other's internals.
beats.fix: Fix a small set of verbs saying what action is intended, a numeric space of replies saying what happened, and a header area for everything else — and define all of it independently of how the bytes are laid out on the wire.
beats.cost: The vocabulary is only as meaningful as the agreement to use it honestly, and because the semantics are version-independent while the wire format is not, performance characteristics change underneath code that is unaware of the difference.

interview.q: What actually changed between the major versions of this protocol?
interview.trap: Answering that the newer versions are faster, or listing features without separating layers. The semantics are identical by design — a method and a status code mean the same thing in every version — and only the framing and connection handling changed.
